football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Virginia Tech, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.0 of the 2.8 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Clemson has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Clemson’s offense has allowed a sack on 8.1% of its dropbacks, and Virginia Tech’s defense sacks the quarterback on 9.6% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).

When Clemson has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Clemson’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 17.5% of its runs, and Virginia Tech’s defense stops 27.8% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
When Clemson has the ball (third down): Clemson’s offense converts 31.9% of its third downs, and Virginia Tech’s defense allows opponents to convert 32.5% of their third downs (FBS average 39.7%).

When Clemson has the ball (big plays through the air): Clemson’s offense turns 7.6% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Virginia Tech’s defense gives up explosive gains on 9.9% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).
contradicting: When Virginia Tech has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Virginia Tech’s offense has allowed a sack on 6.9% of its dropbacks, and Clemson’s defense sacks the quarterback on 7.3% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).

When Virginia Tech has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Virginia Tech’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 21.3% of its runs, and Clemson’s defense stops 16.4% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
